biblical studies, we would refer to this as the text. And frequently the text is a reference to the Hebrew Bible as a
single corpus. What did it originally look like when it first came together as what we would recognize as the Hebrew
Bible? But you can also talk about the text of the individual books of the Bible. And a lot of people seem to think
that when we talk about Genesis or when we talk about Isaiah or when we talk about the Gospel of John that an
individual sat down and wrote out the whole text more or less as we have it today and then it's just been in circulation as that version ever since.
And so a lot of people think that what we have in the Bible today is more or less identical to the text, the
autograph of the text, the original version of the text. Most scholars today, however, would say not only is
such an text not recoverable, but for most of the books of the Bible, no such text ever existed. And what that means
is not that these texts just come out of nowhere, but that there's no version of
Genesis that came from a single pen of a single author in a way that we would recognize as Genesis because the book of
Genesis is a combination of a bunch of different sources. We have the primeval history which itself was probably a combination of multiple different
stories. And then we do know that we have multiple different genealogies that are tracing the same ancestral line. And
then we have the Abraham cycle, the Isaac cycle, the Jacob cycle which probably originally circulated independently before being brought
together. And then when Genesis was combined with other texts from the Pentatuk, there was further editing that took place. And the further back we
trace these individual sources and traditions, the less and less identifiable they become as the book of
Genesis. But additionally, a lot of them probably originally circulated orally.
And they were probably in circulation for generations before anyone ever wrote them down. And so even the original writing down of these texts is not the
original composition of the stories they tell. And there were likely multiple different periods during which these
oral traditions in different stages of their growth were written down. And then those written versions of the different
stages of the growth of these oral traditions could have interacted with each other as well. People could have tried to combine them together and
either weave them together into one single text or use them in different parts of the story so that we have very
very similar stories being told in different parts of for instance the book of Genesis or they might have supplemented one with the other. There
are a variety of different ways that the texts of the Bible have come together.
And the further we go back into searching for an original version of these texts, the more and more different
sources and versions we find and the less and less confident we become in the reality of an original text. And this is
particularly true of books like Genesis and Isaiah and Joshua and Judges and things like that, but also of some New
Testament texts. So the gospel of John has probably undergone quite a bit of editing. A lot of people think Luke came together in a few different stages. And
we also have 2 Corinthians for instance that many scholars think is probably a combination of a few different letters that were written by Paul. So while
there is probably a minority of texts in the Bible that were written once by an original author and more or less come
down to us in a form similar to what was originally written for the majority of texts. There's a long compositional history that includes editing,
redacting, compiling, but then also different stages of growth in their oral circulation and then probably multiple different textualization periods,
multiple different periods where different people were writing them down and then redacting and editing and compiling those written versions. So
again, we can't really talk about an original text of most of the texts of the Bible. We can only talk about sources and those may go back to
original texts but probably go back to oral traditions that were in circulation in a variety of different versions and ways even before they were ever written
down. So this is the complexity of talking about an text and this is why I and other scholars will frequently say that we probably can't even talk about
